newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices fall sharply for second day in row.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices fall sharply for second day in row.

text.p: Coffee futures prices tumbled for a second consecutive session on Monday after hitting two-year highs last week as speculators continued to take profits from the dizzying five-month jump in prices.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on Monday, July futures closed down 22.45 cents a pound at 253.95 cents -- down 20 percent, or 64.05 cents, from Thursday's high of 318 cents, the highest price for coffee since 1977.

But while prices may come under further pressure this week, strong fundamental factors are likely to keep the market well supported, analysts said, and any threat of a frost in top grower Brazil would likely reignite a buying spree.

"The bull market is not dead, but it's got a couple of swords in its back," said Allendale analyst Jim Cordier. "We may have topped out, but the fundamentals are still bullish. Coffee is still in tight supply."
Coffee stockpiles, now near 20-year lows in both consuming and producing countries, are at the root of the dizzying run-up on the futures market since December.

"I think you've had a lot of people get long for the (Brazilian) freeze season," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "May is usually the time for the top to be made -- and it was. Now there's a buying void in this market."

Worries that cold weather could damage coffee trees in Brazil typically fuels buying of coffee ahead of the country's June-through-August winter season. Brazil normally supplies at least a quarter of the world's coffee each year.

With Brazil's two most dangerous cold-weather months coming up and world coffee stocks not expected to build until the next Central American harvest this autumn, some analysts said it may be too soon to predict the market has topped.
"Time-wise, it's too early to call a top," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "The period of tightness is only in front of us."

Ganes said falling prices for Brazilian coffees compared with other Latin American origins and a willingness by roasters to substitute cheaper Brazilian beans for higher-priced coffees were two negative factors now affecting the market.

Analysts also said news on Friday that No. 2 grower Colombia was offering North American roasters about 300,000 60-kilogram (bags of green coffee for June shipment had thrown some cold water on the red-hot market.
"I think exporters in Colombia kicking out more coffee to the United States doesn't change the entire fundamental picture," said Cordier. "But it does alleviate some near-term tightness."

Some analysts also fear that soaring coffee prices will start to hurt consumption. Several rounds of retail price hikes since February have raised the supermarket price for a 13-ounce can of ground coffee by about 50 percent.

"Futures prices over $3 will have an impact on consumption," Platt said. "It may not necessarily have a big impact in the United States, but it will hurt producing and developing countries where consumption has grown the most."
